rashi:a2.1: That he gazes upward: [his eyes] stand in their place in proper order, but they look upward all the time. The ḥeder [room] is below; the aliyya [upper story] is above.
rashi:a3.1: That are situated above: at the height of the forehead, not as with other people.
rashi:a3.2: And they are situated in their order: that is, they stand in their place in order, but he sees the room and the upper story, for one eye sees upward and one eye sees downward.
rashi:a4.1: In his eye: “tevallul in his eye.” It could have written just “dak, tevallul,” and I would know that this applies only to the eye.
rashi:a5.1: A blind man [ish iver]: from the inclusion of the word ish [man].
rashi:a6.1: Blind [iver]: implies that his eyes were taken away and are not there at all.
rashi:a7.1: Impairment [maḥsoraita]: his sight is diminished, but he sees somewhat.
rashi:a7.2: Dak [cataract]: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss.) It diminishes the sight but does not take it away.
rashi:a7.3: Intermingling [mevalbelita]: the white breaks across the rim and enters the black, and it does not shorten the sight at all.
rashi:a8.1: Deviations [meshanyuta]: eyes that are unusual in their position, such as above or below, or seeing the room and the upper story at once.
rashi:a9.1: Dimness [kahyuta]: that he does not see.
rashi:a9.2: Is derived from “man”: for these pale spots and constant tears are a kind of dimness, and the tanna of the baraita derives them from “man.”
rashi:a10.1: Sakhei shemesh: Rav Yosef taught “sanei shemesh”: one who hates the sun and cannot look at a place where the sun is shining.
rashi:a10.2: One of ours and one of theirs: he has one eye like the eye of these who sit opposite me, and one eye like mine. Rav Yehuda was sitting opposite him, and his eyes were unusual.
rashi:a11.1: Shekhavna: whose eyebrows are long and lie over his eyes.
rashi:a12.5: Flowing [toredot]: more than streaming, as in “a continual dripping [delef tored]” (Proverbs 27:15).
rashi:a13.1: It is taught: also the zadir, the lupin and the timyan: it is a blemish, for his eyes are askew.
rashi:a13.2: But does he teach these together with blemishes?: is this timyan [one whose lashes are depleted] a blemish? Our mishna disqualifies him only because of the appearance!
rashi:a13.3: Where the stumps remained: the roots [remain]; then it is not a blemish, only [a disqualification] because of the appearance.
rashi:a14.1: Relative to his limbs: such as his arms, his legs and his shins.
rashi:a14.2: Tzimem, tzime’a: the mishna explains them.
rashi:a14.3: Similar to a sponge: shriveled and closed.
rashi:a15.1: Ten ammot: it was assumed [at first] that he meant by Moses’s own cubit.
rashi:a16.1: A blemished person: for his body is larger than his arms, since no person’s body is more than three cubits by his own cubit.
rashi:a16.2: I was speaking of the cubit of the boards: that is, ten cubits by the cubit of the boards, for the length of the boards was not measured by Moses’s own cubit. And what we said in the previous chapter (Bekhorot 40a), “one longer than that of Moses by half a fingerbreadth,” does not mean Moses’s own cubit literally, for Moses’s own cubit was certainly far longer than the sacred cubit that Moses established.
rashi:a17.1: Like a small finger: if his nose is too large for his other limbs by the measure of the width of a small finger, it is a blemish. How do we gauge it? We measure his nose against the noses of people as tall as he is.
rashi:a18.1: Ḥaziza: its ears are very long, so that they bend downward.
rashi:a20.1: In the Temple: since it is not a blemish.
rashi:a20.2: And the tzime’aḥ, the tzimem and the tzime’a: and our mishna, which counts them [as blemishes in a person], does so because such a one is not like the rest of the offspring of Aaron.
rashi:a21.1: Their core [zakhrut]: that is the bone inserted inside the horns. The core of the hooves is the bone inside the hooves, which is the sole of the foot.
rashi:a21.2: And one may not redeem them: if it is an animal of other offerings, not a firstborn, it is not redeemed for this, since it is not a full blemish, only enough to disqualify it.
rashi:a22.1: And they are redeemed for them: this is difficult for Rav Ḥisda, who said they are not redeemed.
rashi:a22.2: The baraita, which teaches it, is where they were uprooted: the horns and the roots of the core, so that a hollow is visible in the head.
rashi:a22.3: Rav Ḥisda, where they were cut: they were cut from above, and their roots remained.
rashi:a23.1: And where they were cut: does even a disqualification apply to it?
rashi:a23.3: Yagod: he should cut, as in “Hew down [godu] the tree” (Daniel 4:11).
rashi:a23.4: Ze’eiri interpreted it: what it teaches, “he should cut,” means above their core, for at the tip of the horn there are some two or three fingerbreadths that the core does not reach. If the blackness does not reach the place of the core, he may cut it; but beyond that, it is disqualified.
tosafot:a10.1: Rav Huna pointed: one of theirs: that is, of Rav Yehuda, who was before him. Rashi explained that his eyes were unusual, but did not explain how they were unusual. Rabbeinu Tam explains: Rav Yehuda was the tallest man of his generation, as it says in chapter HaMapelet (Nidda 24b), and Rav Huna was a short man, as is stated in tractate Ta’anit, in the chapter about the pious. Therefore [Rav Huna’s] eyes did not look noticeably smaller than those of ordinary people, but next to Rav Yehuda’s they did, for his were very large. That is why Rav Yehuda took offense. And this is the “difference”: one eye large and one small. And even though this is not a blemish that would profane the service unless the eye is as large as a calf’s or as small as a goose’s, nonetheless such a one is not like the rest of the offspring of Aaron.
tosafot:a12.1: His eyes are terutot: Rashi explained “round,” as in “for it is terutah” in Sanhedrin (107), said of the moon; and tziraniyyot, Rashi explained, rounder than terutot. This is puzzling: once he teaches the lighter case, all the more so the more severe one! The same difficulty arises where he teaches dome’ot, dolfot and toredot, since dolfot is more than dome’ot and toredot is more than dolfot. Perhaps it was necessary to teach them all to tell us that they are disqualified not as a blemish but because such a one is not like the rest of the offspring of Aaron.
gershom:a1.1: In his eye: as it is written, “or tevallul in his eye.”
gershom:a2.1: That are not there at all: his eyes.
gershom:a3.1: But impairment [maḥsoraita]: where the sight of his eyes is somewhat diminished, the Merciful One wrote dak, and that is maḥsoraita; but intermingling [mevalbelita], no: where the white is mixed into the black.
gershom:a4.1: But deviations: where the look of his eyes is unusual.
gershom:a5.1: Dimness [kahyuta]: that he does not see at all.
gershom:a6.1: Sakhei shemesh: Rav Yosef taught that this is sanei shemesh, one who cannot look at the sunlight.
gershom:a7.1: Zagdim: Rav Huna pointed: one of ours and one of theirs. That is, one of his eyes is healthy, like ours, and the other is like those of people whose eyes are unusual.
gershom:a8.1: And Rav Yehuda took offense: because he was like that. [The note ends with a few words, “vegeres shekhavya hatzeiri,” which seem to give Rabbeinu Gershom’s reading of the next lemmas, shekhavna and hatzayran; the printed text is unclear.]
gershom:a10.1: Tziraniyyot: the place where the eye sits is round.
gershom:a12.1: Toredot: that drip without stopping. And some say toredot means that he can close his eyes only with great effort. [The note runs on into the next baraita:] Zivver: whose eyes are askew. [A garbled word follows, apparently:] his eyes are hidden.
gershom:a13.1: Lupin: whose lashes are many; the hairs of his eyelids are large.
gershom:a14.1: And the timin, whose lashes are gone: who has no eyelashes at all.
gershom:a15.1: It is not difficult: those that the outside tanna [of the baraita] adds are where stumps remained; that is, even though the root remained, it disqualifies. [Rabbeinu Gershom pairs the two cases the opposite way from Rashi and the English translation.]
gershom:a16.1: And that one, of our mishna: where no stumps remained at all.
gershom:a17.1: Shimi, I was speaking of the sacred cubit: that Moses our teacher was ten cubits [by that cubit]; by his own cubits he was only three cubits, like every person, who is three of his own cubits tall.
gershom:a18.1: It is taught: up to the thickness of a small finger [it is fit]; beyond that, smaller or larger, is a blemish.
gershom:a19.1: Similar to a sponge: bunched together.
gershom:a20.1: A gadya ḥaziza: whose ears hang down.
gershom:a21.1: And their core with them: the bone inside; it is disqualified from being offered.
gershom:a22.1: This is where they were cut: some of their core remained, so it is not redeemed for them.
gershom:a23.1: A red heifer whose horns are black at the tip: he should saw off that black part with a saw, and it is fit. He holds [this] even though he cut into their core.
gershom:a24.1: No: Ze’eiri interpreted it: he cut above their core, and so it is not disqualified.
rashi:b1.2: An epileptic [nikhpe]: one who falls because of illness.
rashi:b1.3: Once in a while: he falls only once in a while, at a fixed time.
rashi:b1.4: A melancholy temper [ruaḥ ketzara]: a demon’s spirit.
rashi:b1.6: Ba’al gever: his member is large.
rashi:b2.1: And they may not drink water: for it is the way of a Torah scholar to be modest in eating and drinking; but in urinating he should not be modest, lest he wait and endanger himself.
rashi:b3.1: It was necessary for him: to urinate.
rashi:b3.2: On the Shabbat of the Festival: [in the] thirty days before the Festival, when people ask and expound the halakhot of the Festival, as we say in Megilla (4a).
rashi:b3.3: They spread a cloak for him: they spread a sheet between him and the people.
rashi:b3.4: Retract the incident: expound that it is forbidden to hold back from urinating until one has privacy.
rashi:b3.5: You, who can: have a sheet spread, because you are important.
rashi:b3.6: But if another person needed to and could not, he would wait until the people left, and endanger himself, and become barren.
rashi:b4.2: In her ear: even into her ear I would urinate, if I had no other place, rather than wait; all the more so in front of her.
rashi:b5.1: And let me derive it from a leech: it was taught above that he sought to urinate and did not, and his belly was found swollen. From where [do we know] that this came from the waiting? Perhaps he swallowed a leech (Rashi adds an Old French gloss), and that is why his belly swelled.
rashi:b5.2: Where it drips: he cannot urinate properly afterward, only drop by drop; that certainly came from holding back the urine.
rashi:b7.1: At a time that you are as among your cattle: when you make yourself like an animal, not being modest about urinating.
rashi:b8.1: That your prayer will not be barren, etc.: when you pray [for children], your prayer will be heard.
rashi:b8.2: As an animal: that you do not hold back from urinating.
rashi:b9.1: Not on an earthenware vessel: into a chamber pot, because they throw it into a nearby river, and the rivers of Babylonia flow on and collect at Ein Eitam, as is explained.
rashi:b9.2: Nor on a hard place: which does not absorb; [the urine] floats on the ground until it is washed down a slope and falls into the river.
rashi:b9.3: And Rav says, those inclines of Babylonia: the sloping places in Babylonia.
rashi:b9.4: Return [the water] to Ein Eitam: where the High Priest immersed on Yom Kippur, as we say in tractate Yoma, chapter three (31a).
rashi:b9.5: Should not stand openly in front of a child: when she urinates, she should not stand directly facing the children, for that is brazen.
rashi:b9.6: Sideways: if [she turns] to the other side, so that she does not urinate facing the child, we have no problem with it.
rashi:b10.2: Hidrokan: an illness of the intestines.
rashi:b10.4: Much blood, many boils: one who has much blood and does not let blood gets many boils.
rashi:b10.5: Much semen: one who has a wife and does not have relations with her gets much leprosy.
rashi:b11.1: A spirit of folly has seized [him], through a demon; this is ben nefilim (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:b12.1: The kayyan: that is the meshuban.
rashi:b12.2: The garbetan: that is a kind of ba’al gever.
rashi:b12.3: In the testicles: his testicles are large.
rashi:b12.4: In the member: his member is large.
rashi:b13.1: And how much: must the member grow for him to be disqualified?
rashi:b14.1: Whose testicles were crushed: his testicles were crushed [nimoḥu].
rashi:b14.2: That has wind in his testicles: his testicles are swollen.
rashi:b14.3: Whose appearance is dark: he is black like a Kushite. And [the verse] does not speak of the testicles at all.
rashi:b15.1: It is difficult for Rabbi Yishmael: that is, this is why Rabbi Yishmael disagrees with the first tanna: it is difficult for him that if the verse speaks of one who has no testicles, it should have said ḥasar ashekh.
rashi:b15.2: He teaches, whose testicles were crushed: this is why Rabbi Yishmael teaches “whose testicles were crushed.”
rashi:b15.3: It should have said mimro’aḥ ashekh: for the mem of mero’aḥ is a servile letter [a prefix, not part of the root].
rashi:b16.1: Subtract and add: they subtract the ḥet from mero’aḥ and the alef from ashekh, and add a ḥet in place of the alef to ashekh and an alef in place of the ḥet to mero’aḥ, and it becomes mar’o ḥoshekh [his appearance is dark].
rashi:b17.1: This is the Kushite: and the mishna below (45a) [printed on our daf on 45b] teaches the Kushite explicitly: “the kushi and the giḥor.”
rashi:b18.1: One who knocks his ankles: his knees are bent outward and his ankles inward, and they knock against each other as he walks. And “his knees” is the reverse: his legs are bent outward and he keeps them apart, until his knees, which bend inward above, knock against each other.
tosafot:b2.1: And they may not drink water in public: Rashi explained that it is the way of Torah scholars to be modest in eating and drinking. As for what is said at the end of Keitzad Tzolin (Pesaḥim 86b), that Rav Huna son of Rav Natan drank a cup in two draughts without turning his face away, and he said there, “We learned [this rule only of] a bride,” which implies that it is customary to drink in public without turning one’s face: that is at a meal, like a bride. And in Hilkhot Derekh Eretz we say that in public he should turn his face to another side and drink. It seems that it mentions water because not everyone usually drinks water, only one who is thirsty, whereas other drinks people usually drink together. Rabbeinu Tam says it means this: even for those modest people who do not drink water in public, one should not be modest about urinating, lest he wait and endanger himself.
tosafot:b7.1: When will there not be a barren male or female among you? At a time that [you are] as among your cattle: This is puzzling: how could they make themselves like an animal in urinating, when they had to go outside the camp and go three parasangs away, as we say in the last chapter of Yoma (75b), and they relieved themselves neither to their sides nor in front of them, only behind them? And this applies even to urinating, for in chapter Mi Shemetu (Berakhot 25a) the verse “And you shall have a place outside the camp, and you shall go out there” is explained as referring to urine.
tosafot:b8.1: That your prayer will not be barren before the Omnipresent, at a time when you make yourself as an animal: Rashi explained that it will not be barren when you pray for children. But it seems that it speaks of every prayer, as it says that the world endures only for the sake of one who makes himself like an animal, as it is written: “Man and beast You preserve, O Lord,” and for the sake of one who makes himself as if he is nothing, as it is written: “He hangs the earth upon nothing [belima]” (Job 26:7) (Ḥullin 89a).
tosafot:b9.1: A person should not urinate on an earthenware vessel or on a hard place: These stringencies apply only in Babylonia, since the reason given is that those inclines of Babylonia return the water to Eitam, on the Euphrates, for the water flows along its course to Ein Eitam, because the Euphrates mixes with all the waters in the world, as it says below in chapter 9 (Bekhorot 55a): one who vows not to benefit from the waters of the Euphrates is forbidden all the waters in the world. And even springs that rise up, we say below, are offshoots of the Euphrates; and in Sukka (53a) too we say, “Let us dig a little and seek water”: those are offshoots of the Euphrates. Even though the offshoots of the Euphrates mix with all the waters in the world, it is forbidden only in Babylonia, as I explained, since the Euphrates’ course mixes into Ein Eitam. From here it would seem that the Euphrates flows from Babylonia to the Land of Israel. But I asked someone from the Land of Israel, and he told me that it flows down from the Land of Israel to Babylonia. So it is also evident below in chapter 9 (Bekhorot 55b), where we say: “Of rain in the West [the Land of Israel], the Euphrates is the great witness,” and so Rashi explained there. And it is strained to say that even though it flows from Babylonia to the Land of Israel, [the rain] shows when the river rises from heavy rains and swells backward from the abundance of water.
tosafot:b9.2: This woman should not stand openly in front of a child: even though she does not expose herself, it is brazen when she urinates with the child standing in front of her, for it is not the way of a woman to expose herself before anyone, neither children nor adults, as is evident in chapter Mi Shemetu (Berakhot 23b).
tosafot:b10.1: Brings him to dropsy [hidrokan] … brings him to jaundice [yerakon]: this implies that hidrokan and yerakon are two different things. Yet it seems they are one matter, for we say in Yevamot (60b): they passed them before the [High Priest’s] frontplate, and any girl fit for intercourse, her face turned yellow [morikot]; and it says, a sign of transgression is hidrokan.
gershom:b1.1: An epileptic, even once in a while: that is, even if [he falls only] at a fixed time, he is disqualified for the service even on the other days, when he does not fall.
gershom:b2.1: They urinate in public: for it is dangerous to hold oneself back. And they do not drink water in public: for that is not proper manners [derekh eretz].
gershom:b3.1: And his belly was found tzava: swollen.
gershom:b4.1: It was necessary for him: [to pass] urine.
gershom:b5.1: They spread a cloak for him: to separate him from the people, for the sake of modesty.
gershom:b6.1: He came [and] told his father how they had spread a cloak.
gershom:b7.1: He said to him: I will give you four hundred zuz, and go and set the incident right. That is, establish the matter according to its halakha: urinate before them openly, so that they will not learn from you to endanger themselves by holding back.
gershom:b8.1: You: who have a cloak, can spread it. But one who cannot, since he has no cloak to spread, will hold himself back and be endangered.
gershom:b9.1: In her ear: that is, I would urinate even in her ear before I would endanger myself.
gershom:b10.1: And let me derive it from a leech: that is, that his belly was swollen not because of urine but because he swallowed a leech.
gershom:b11.1: Where it drips: the urine; for had he swallowed a leech, it would not drip.
gershom:b12.1: At the time when a person needs: and holds himself back, they are punctured.
gershom:b13.1: At a time that [you are] as among your cattle: when you make yourself like an animal, which urinates in front of many, there will be no barren male or female among you.
gershom:b14.1: When: is your prayer not barren, when you pray about children? At a time when you make yourself like an animal, not holding yourself back.
gershom:b15.1: Those inclines of Babylonia: the slopes of Babylonia. If one urinates on them, the urine flows back to Ein Eitam, to the river that runs toward the Land of Israel, and people would drink from it. Therefore he should urinate only on a low place, so that it is absorbed there [and does not reach] the spring.
gershom:b16.1: Should not stand openly in front of a child: when she urinates, for the sake of modesty. Sideways, when she turns her face away, we have no problem with it.
gershom:b17.1: Hidrokan: that is, his belly is swollen.
gershom:b19.1: Much blood: when he holds back and does not let blood.
gershom:b20.1: Many boils: that is, he is stricken with boils.
gershom:b21.1: A ruaḥ ketzarot comes upon him: which the mishna taught is a blemish. What is it? A spirit of folly has seized [him].
gershom:b22.1: Ben nefalim: a demon’s spirit; madness.
gershom:b23.1: The meshukhan and the ba’al garav [so Rabbeinu Gershom’s text reads, for meshuban and ba’al gever]: meshukhan in the testicles, whose testicles are exceedingly large.
gershom:b24.1: Ba’al garav [read: gever]: in the member, which is exceedingly long.
gershom:b25.1: He pointed: Rav Yehuda [indicated] that the member is long down to the knee.
gershom:b26.1: Whose testicles were crushed: his testicles were crushed [nimoḥu].
gershom:b27.1: That has wind in his testicles: his testicles are swollen.
gershom:b28.1: Whose appearance is dark: he is black like a Kushite.
gershom:b29.1: It is difficult for Rabbi Yishmael: if it were as the first tanna says, it should have said ḥasar ashekh; so he teaches, “whose testicles were crushed.” And likewise what Rabbi Yishmael said is difficult for Rabbi Akiva. Each one seeks to answer [with] his own reasoning.
gershom:b30.1: He holds: Rabbi Ḥanina holds that one subtracts, adds and expounds. One subtracts the [alef] from ashekh and adds it in mero’aḥ, which becomes mar’eh [appearance]; and one subtracts the ḥet from mero’aḥ and adds it in place of the alef in ashekh, which becomes ḥoshekh [dark]. That is mar’o ḥoshekh: whose appearance is dark.
gershom:b31.1: One who knocks his ankles and his knees: when he walks, his ankles or his knees knock against each other; and that is the hakishan we speak of in the Gemara.
